report:
Based on the evidence, here is my conclusion:

**Conclusion: Largely supported, but with important qualifications.**

The most robust evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis by Kappelmann et al. (2018, *Molecular Psychiatry*), which pooled clinical trials of anti-cytokine drugs (mainly anti-TNF agents, anti-IL-6 antibodies like tocilizumab, and IL-12/23 inhibitors) used for chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and Crohn's disease. Depression was typically a secondary outcome. The meta-analysis found a small-to-moderate but statistically significant reduction in depressive symptoms with anti-cytokine treatment compared to placebo, independent of improvement in the underlying physical disease severity, suggesting a direct antidepressant effect (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/).

However, when anti-cytokine drugs (particularly infliximab, a TNF antagonist) have been tested directly as treatments for depression itself—rather than as treatments for inflammatory disease with depression as a secondary measure—results are more mixed. Raison et al.'s randomized controlled trial of infliximab in treatment-resistant depression found no overall antidepressant effect, though a subgroup with elevated baseline inflammatory markers (high CRP) did show benefit (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7244402/). A more recent proof-of-mechanism trial similarly found effects concentrated in motivational/anhedonia domains among highly inflamed patients rather than broad depressive symptoms (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-024-02751-x).

**Bottom line:** In people being treated for chronic inflammatory diseases, anti-cytokine drugs are associated with modest reductions in depressive symptoms, but the effect appears most reliable in patients with elevated baseline inflammation, and is not a universal antidepressant effect across all depressed individuals.
